questions.prompt: Which properties should a good unit test have? Select all that apply.

options.text: Small scope — exercises one piece of code
Talks to the real production database

questions.explanation: Unit tests are small, fast, and deterministic; hitting a real database makes a test slow and flaky — not a unit test.

questions.prompt: Why are pure functions the easiest code to unit-test?

options.text: They always run on the network
Their output depends only on inputs and they have no side effects, so you just assert the return value

questions.explanation: Same inputs → same output with no side effects means no setup, doubles, or cleanup — just pass inputs and check the result.

questions.prompt: A solitary unit test differs from a sociable one because it:

options.text: Replaces the unit's collaborators with test doubles

questions.explanation: Solitary tests isolate the unit by swapping collaborators for doubles; sociable tests use the real collaborators.

questions.prompt: Anything a function does beyond returning a value — writing a file, calling the network, mutating global state — is a ____ ____.
questions.explanation: Side effects make code harder to test; pushing logic into pure functions keeps side effects thin and at the edges.

questions.prompt: Match each input category to an edge case worth testing for a list-processing function.

pairs.right: The min or max allowed value (off-by-one)
A negative count where positive is expected

questions.explanation: Bugs cluster at empties, single-vs-many, boundaries, and invalid inputs — test each deliberately.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to make tangled I/O-plus-logic code easy to unit-test.

items.text: Extract the decision logic into a pure function
Leave a thin caller that does the I/O
Unit-test the pure function with in-memory data

questions.explanation: Separate logic from I/O, keep the side-effecting caller thin, then test the pure core directly.
